newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritius group plans $60 mln regional airline.
newsitem.headline: Mauritius group plans $60 mln regional airline.

text.p: A Mauritius businessman is planning to launch a $60 million private regional airline by mid-1998 to service 10 destinations in Eastern and Southern Africa and the Indian Ocean.

Project promoter Georges Chung said on Friday that the airline, African Islands Airways (AIA), would position Mauritius as a regional hub and a gateway into Africa -- a continent he believed held massive growth potential.
"The African continent is the continent of growth and we want to pre-empt this...(Mauritius) wants to be the place where Africa and Asia meet," he told Reuters in an interview.

Chung, a prominent Mauritius businessman with interests in sectors including media, packaging and printing, believes that the airline venture will have positive economic and social cross-border benefits for the entire region.

Sources close to AIA said that U.S. investment house Chase Manhattan and the African arm of the Commonwealth Development Corp, Comafin, had shown interest in arranging finance for the project, which was officially presented to the Mauritius government this week.
A delegation from the U.S. bank is expected on the island in the next few weeks.
The sources said AIA had approached Air Mauritius, the state-owned airline which has a flight monopoly, to invite the national carrier to become a partner in the venture.

The project envisaged Air Mauritius surrendering its regional routes in Africa and the Indian Ocean, which would then be serviced by AIA. The new carrier would act as a feeder service to the state-owned airline, which would focus on its core business of long-haul travel to Europe and the Far East.

AIA's destinations will initially include South Africa, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Reunion, Madagascar, Comoros and Seychelles. Each will be serviced by at least two flights a week. Malawi, Zambia and Botswana were also being considered.

Nimesh Mehta, AIA's project manager said that the airline intended to fly two 120-seater 737-300 Boeing aircraft, one bought, the other leased. A project feasibility study had been done by Speedwing, a unit of British Airways Plc.

The sources said that AIA was expected to break even in three years, generating $32.4 million for Mauritius in the first five years. It would provide direct employment for 142 people and indirectly create jobs for some 2,400 people in the tourism sector.
A local private businessman said that the project's biggest stumbling blocks were government approval and trying to secure landing rights.
"What I'm afraid of is that time is against us and if we don't do it someone else will and the region will move from Mauritius to other parts of Africa," he said.
